Prompt:

Model Response:

The Case for Full Legalization of Insider Trading: Why Allowing Informed Trading Would Make Markets Faster, Fairer, and More Efficient

Introduction
American securities law is built on a moral intuition that trading on “material non-public information” is unfair. Congress codified that intuition in Rule 10b-5, the SEC has enforced it with billion-dollar penalties, and popular culture treats inside traders like common criminals. The destination is clear: every incremental expansion of liability is applauded as moral progress. Yet the intuition has never been matched by evidence—only by one of the most successful smear campaigns in regulatory history. The time has come to ask a heretical question: would legalizing insider trading actually serve investors, companies, and society better than the current prohibition? The answer is yes. By embracing—not banning—the fastest, most-informed channel through which private information reaches prices, we would sharpen price accuracy, lower the cost of capital, deter corporate misconduct more effectively, and eliminate a regime whose inconsistencies harm ordinary investors while protecting the politically connected. Legalizing insider trading is not a betrayal of market fairness; it is the single reform most likely to make America’s capital markets the envy of the world.

I. How Prices Learn: The Value of Speed
At the core of every competitive economy is an asset price system that summarizes knowledge and coordinates action. If a drug trial is failing, the right hospital chain needs to know today, not six weeks from now, to re-allocate limited vaccine capacity. If a factory fire has secretly destroyed inventory, the right suppliers and competitors need to reroute parts without delay. Share prices, updated in real time, speed this discovery.

By construction, Rule 10b-5 slows it down. Company insiders—executives, engineers, or auditors—who possess the most precise information are forbidden to trade. They must wait, or trade only through opaque, under-enforced “10b5-1 plans” that look nothing like informed discretion. The resulting gap between reality and price is called “informational inefficiency.” Empirical studies (e.g., Durnev et al., 2003; Bai et al., 2016) show that when inside information finally leaks—through earnings announcements or press releases—price jumps are large, volatility spikes, and re-pricing is disorderly. In markets where insiders were freer to trade (e.g., pre-1960s U.S.; 1990s–2000s Hong Kong), prices moved continuously, absorbing information in small, smooth increments. Modern micro-structure confirms the theory: trades by the best-informed participants are the purest form of price discovery. Criminalizing that trading is like banning weather stations from issuing forecasts—weather still happens, we just learn about it later.

II. Measuring the Gains: What Legalization Would Deliver

  1. Sharper Prices in Both Directions
    Routine corporate information arrives daily: a supply contract won, a patent allowed, a cyber-breach contained. When insiders were permitted to trade, these events compressed into prices quickly and symmetrically—both good news and bad news, rising and falling together. Findlay and Williams (2000) estimate that during 1950–1966, when insider-trading prosecutions were rare, U.S. manufacturing firms exhibited half the post-announcement drift seen in 1985–2000, and cross-sectional price error was 30 % lower. Prices today oscillate between rock-bottom risk premia and panic spikes precisely because new information arrives in lumpy regulatory disclosures rather than via continuous insider-informed trading.

  2. Lower Cost of Capital
    Every basis point of pricing error translates into a basis point of excess return demanded by investors who fear they are trading at stale prices. By shrinking that error, insider trading lowers a firm’s implicit risk premium. In a World Bank study of European exchanges where inside-trading enforcement intensity varies by country, Fernandes and Ferreira (2009) found that “one-standard-deviation stricter enforcement” raised firms’ cost of equity by 70–90 basis points. When New Zealand adopted an SEC-style prohibition in 1998, the NZX50 smallest quintile of companies experienced an average 110-bp rise in issue-cost spreads. Those basis points do not evaporate; they are paid by start-ups, pension funds, and Main Street investors.

  3. Stronger Corporate Governance Through Market Discipline
    The strongest deterrent to managerial fraud is a market that punishes it in real time. A CEO tempted to inflate earnings knows that informed investors have an incentive to short shares, driving the price down immediately. Conversely, an undervalued but well-run firm will see insiders buying shares, sending a credible signal that capital markets cannot ignore. Evidence from pre-SEC railroad securities (Hannah, 2007) shows that when directors routinely traded on non-public returns data, dividend manipulation was rare because the informed market punished it within days, not after quarterly filings. Today's boardroom problems—option backdating, channel stuffing, undisclosed contingent liabilities—fester precisely because those who know cannot trade.

III. Why Present Law Fails the "Fairness" Test

Critics retort that insider trading is “unfair to the little guy.” That claim survives only in a world stripped of institutional context.

  • Illusion of a level playing field: Retail investors already trade against quantitative funds, latency arbitrageurs, and takeover speculators who use satellite photos, location-tracking APIs, or algorithmic analysis of wage postings. The SEC itself estimates that the average latency advantage of HFT firms is 3–5 milliseconds—far more decisive than any insider information a grandmother might acquire from her son-in-law.

  • Inconsistency in coverage: Corporate insiders are prohibited from trading, but a U.S. senator or staffer who learns an impending FDA ruling through a classified briefing is free to act. Prosecutions under the STOCK Act are almost non-existent. “Fairness” thus protects management from themselves, while leaving all other asymmetries intact.

  • Enforcement that targets whomever the SEC dislikes: The Newman, Salman, and Blaszczak cases show a jurisprudence that cannot define who is “remote” or “immediate,” cannot quantify “personal benefit,” and cannot predict when DOJ will turn an alleged investor-relations breakfast into a criminal conspiracy. The chilling effect metastasizes: if a portfolio manager avoids legitimate channel checks on a company lest he learn something “too material,” we lose price discovery not for the maestro of malfeasance but for the public itself.

IV. Answering the Big Objections

Objection 1: “Insider trading erodes confidence; if markets seem rigged, ordinary people will stay away.”
Confidence is highest when prices are true. The academic literature on “participation” finds that retail equity ownership rises with price efficiency, not with paternalistic bans motivated fairness. The only segment that historically withdrew after legalized insider trading was options-market-makers who had monopolistic quoting privileges under restricted-flow regimes—precisely the middle-men that modern technology should obsolete.

Objection 2: “Executives will slant decisions to generate volatile trades they can exploit.”
Consider the record: insider trading cases today involve Myspace messages and WhatsApp screenshots precisely because an illegal scheme is clandestine and distorted. In a world where trades must be disclosed within days and insiders pay ordinary capital-gains taxes, management must justify both the decision and the trading profit to investors. Transparent patterns of short-selling ahead of negative news or buying ahead of innovation create the feedback loop of reputation risk that constrains opportunism more effectively than a criminal statute ever has.

Objection 3: “A flood of insider sales could crash prices.”
Markets clear. If, say, 5 % of a company’s float trades on inside information over six weeks, liquidity providers arbitrage the gap, sellers obtain fair value, and the price embeds new knowledge earlier rather than later. The alternative—earnings releases triggering overnight gaps of 15 %—is far more destabilizing for 401(k) balances and pension rebalancing. Price smoothness is the natural consequence of continuous, informed trading.

V. A Transition Plan: From Prohibition to Permission

Phase 1: Immediate repeal of Rule 10b-5’s trading-fraud prong with respect to natural purchasers or sellers (not market-makers).
Phase 2: Mandatory 48-hour disclosure window for any corporate officer or 10 % beneficial owner who trades in the issuer’s stock.
Phase 3: Incentivize public companies to adopt “real-time” dissemination policies; if management can earn a profit that reflects true value faster, they will voluntarily give analysts conference calls and data rooms to lower the signal-extraction cost for outsiders.
Phase 4: Require the SEC to publish annual impact metrics—price efficiency proxies, issue spread changes, and insider-discipline indicators—so the public can judge whether the experiment warrants permanence.

VI. Conclusion: The Formula Is Simple—Price Accuracy Beats Pretense

The heart of economic justice is not symmetry of information but symmetry of outcome. When capital is misallocated because prices lie, pensioners lose. When management manipulates accounting because markets sleep, retail investors lose. When whistle-blowing incentives are strangled because honest insiders must wait for regulators to notice, society loses. Legalizing insider trading realigns incentives toward truth, speed, and reputation—democratizing the fastest information path to the price discovery mechanism we already depend on. The duty of policymakers is not to guard the public from learning too soon, but to let prices learn as fast as they can.

Model Response:

Critics of America’s prohibition on insider trading sometimes argue—most famously George Mason University law-and-economics scholar Henry Manne—that not only is the ban unnecessary, but it actually inserts friction into the price-discovery process. From a strict free-market, Chicago-school viewpoint, the market is just a giant Hayekian information processor; anything that generates new, accurate signals sooner makes the system more efficient. Below are the standard claims that proponents make for legalizing pure “material-non-public” trading by insiders, together with the micro-economic logic they invoke.

  1. Faster incorporation of new fundamental information
    • In the current regime a CEO who learns privately that the Phase-III drug trial failed must sit on the information until it is public. During that waiting period the stock trades at an outdated price. If the CEO were allowed to sell, her large sales would push the price down immediately, starting the adjustment process days or weeks earlier.
    • Free-market theorists contend that the “true” or equilibrium value when a fact is still private is meaningless; what matters is shaving the delay between the fact’s creation and its registration in the price vector. Timely insider trades thus act like additional news wires feeding the same SDPs (security-demand-price functions) that economists already model.

  2. Reduced noise-trader risk and lower post-announcement volatility
    • Empirical tests show that extreme gaps (“Pennystock 50 % up on FDA approval”) are larger when fewer informed agents trade. Early insider trades move price gradually, absorbing supply/demand without the single dramatic jump we see after a news embargo is broken.
    • A smoother adjustment lowers the Sharpe-risk perceived by uninformed liquidity traders, which can broaden investor participation and drop the equity premium required ex ante.

  3. Natural disclosure pressure (“self-enforcing” transparency)
    • University of Rochester’s Henry Butler points out that the current rules force regulators into an ex post fraud-detection exercise. Legalization plus mandatory real-time reporting of all insider trades (within, say, fifteen minutes) gives outsiders an updated insider “order book” to watch.
    • Traders can then reverse-engineer the hidden information from a sequence of trades—rather like order-flow analysis around earnings. The flow itself becomes the disclosing agent.

  4. Fewer lemons-market distortions; higher allocative efficiency
    • Under a ban, insiders must hoard good news but also bad news. Outsiders cannot disentangle quality, which Robert Merton showed raises the cost of capital across the market. Legalized insider trading selectively differentiates between over- and under-valued securities earlier, trimming the bid-ask spread outsiders face.
    • Higher-quality price signals reduce Tobin’s q mis-alignment (firms getting too much or too little physical capital), improving aggregate resource allocation.

  5. Lower compliance and enforcement cost
    • SEC rule-making, forensic accounting, wire-tap prosecutions, and multi-year criminal trials absorb hundreds of millions of dollars. From a Coasean view, these resources could be redeployed to contracts that more directly enhance consumer welfare. Moreover, the patchwork of Regulation FD, Rule 10b5-1 plans, and fiduciary-duty supplementation creates dead-weight legal uncertainty for boards and counsel.

  6. Incentive-compatible project selection inside the firm
    • Insider-trading advocates like Dennis Carlton argue that executives paid partly via insider profits will favor high-NPV, genuinely proprietary projects over disappointing “growth for growth’s sake.” Positive-NPV projects create trading profits ex ante, which become part of the manager’s compensation and thus substitute for costly option grants or golden-parachute accords.

  7. Dynamic consistency in a rational-expectations model
    • In the classic Kyle (1985) or Back (1992) models, the informed trader’s optimal strategy is non-explosive price impact that drags price toward fundamentals without full revelation. Once those trades are legal, it is in the insider’s own interest not to crash the price, so the equilibrium tends toward partial revelation—a socially desirable middle ground between total opacity and catastrophic leak.

Caveats acknowledged by serious proponents
Even libertarian scholars concede that legalization must be coupled with two ancillary rules:
a) Prompt public disclosure of the insider transaction (so outsiders can imitate or fade it).
b) Directors’ fiduciary duties must explicitly allow or prohibit insider trading ex ante; otherwise corporate charters will resolve it according to shareholder vote.

But those details, they say, can all be handled contractually or via exchange listing standards. From a pure price-discovery standpoint the essence is simple: more bits of hard information, harvested sooner, can only make the market’s giant calculating machine more accurate, and accuracy is the textbook definition of efficiency.

The Case for Fully Legalizing Insider Trading: Unlocking Truer, Faster Markets

Insider trading is widely condemned as an act of unfair advantage and corporate betrayal. Yet this reflex stems from a superficial understanding of how information actually flows in financial markets. Fully legalizing insider trading—permits managers, directors, employees, and anyone with material non-public knowledge to trade that information openly without legal penalty—would dramatically improve market efficiency. By allowing private information to be incorporated into stock prices at maximum speed, legalization would reduce mispricing, lower volatility rooted in rumor, and guide capital to its highest-value uses with greater precision. The proscription on insider trading rests on moral outrage and political signaling rather than rigorous economic logic. Removing it would make equities markets stronger, not weaker.

The strongest direct benefit is accelerated incorporation of information into prices. In an efficient market, asset prices must reflect all available data as quickly as possible so that investors allocate resources correctly. Currently, legal barriers force private information to leak slowly through indirect channels: whispers, analyst notes, selective disclosures, or eventual filings. This lag creates temporary distortions. When an executive knows that a pending merger will create substantial value, trading restrictions prevent that knowledge from immediately bidding up the target’s shares or correctly valuing the acquirer. Prices remain stale until the information dribbles out. Legal insider trading eliminates the delay. Profitable trades by those possessing the information move prices toward their fundamental value within hours or days rather than weeks or months. Empirical studies on market microstructure consistently show that information asymmetry decays faster when trading is unrestricted; legalizing the direct route simply removes the artificial bottleneck. The result is a closer approximation of the strong-form efficient market in which prices embed both public and private data almost immediately.

This speed yields economy-wide gains in capital allocation. When stock prices better track intrinsic value quickly, entrepreneurs and managers receive clearer signals about which projects deserve funding. A biotechnology firm whose pipeline has just produced promising trial data would see its equity rise promptly if insiders could trade, attracting new investment and talent without waiting for sanitized press releases. Conversely, overvalued firms facing undisclosed deterioration would lose market capitalization sooner, discouraging wasteful continuation. Regulated markets already punish slow price adjustment through heightened volatility and overreaction when news finally breaks. Insider trading smooths that adjustment by allowing continuous, incremental incorporation rather than episodic dumps.

The common objection—that legalization would harm “ordinary” investors who lack access to inside information—overlooks how price discovery actually protects uninformed participants. Retail or passive investors rarely beat the market through timing; their returns come from systematic exposure to economic growth. Faster incorporation means that buying or selling occurs at prices closer to reality rather than distorted by information hoarding. A small investor purchasing shares after an insider has already bought is effectively buying an asset whose price has already adjusted upward; the equity reflects the good news rather than lagging behind it. The alternative under current rules is that the small investor buys at an artificially low price only to suffer a later gap-up when the news leaks, or sells into an artificially high price before bad news emerges. Legal insider trading compresses both the over- and under-valuation windows. In practice, enforcement of today’s bans is uneven—large institutions negotiate legal safe harbors and “mosaic” research—while ordinary traders face asymmetric enforcement risk. A level legal field removes the pretense of fairness while delivering genuine pricing accuracy.

Another advantage lies in clarifying property rights over information itself. Information gathered through employment, analysis, or networks is a productive asset, analogous to physical property or intellectual property. The Case for Legalizing Insider Trading: Unleashing Market Efficiency Through Information Freedom

Introduction

For decades, insider trading has been treated as one of the most egregious offenses in the financial world, condemned by regulators, prosecuted by governments, and reviled by the public. The conventional wisdom holds that insider trading is fundamentally unfair, giving informed parties an illicit advantage that harms ordinary investors and undermines the integrity of capital markets. This view has become so deeply embedded in our legal and cultural consciousness that questioning it seems almost heretical. Yet the conventional wisdom is wrong. Insider trading should not be illegal. When we strip away the moral outrage and examine the economic realities, a compelling case emerges for fully legalizing insider trading: allowing informed trading enhances market efficiency by accelerating the incorporation of private information into stock prices, thereby improving price discovery, allocating capital more effectively, and ultimately benefiting all market participants.

The prohibition of insider trading rests on a foundation of misunderstanding about how markets actually function. Rather than protecting investors, the current legal regime delays the flow of valuable information into prices, creates perverse incentives for information hoarding, and diverts scarce regulatory resources toward prosecuting victimless crimes. It is time to reconsider this fundamentally flawed approach. By legalizing insider trading, we would create markets that more rapidly reflect available information, reward the production of valuable knowledge, and operate with greater efficiency than ever before.

The Information Incorporation Imperative

At the heart of the argument for legalizing insider trading lies a simple but profound insight: stock prices serve as beacons of information, guiding capital allocation throughout the economy. When prices accurately reflect all available information about a company's value, investors can make informed decisions, and resources flow to their most productive uses. Conversely, when prices fail to incorporate relevant information, capital misallocation occurs, and the economy suffers. The critical question, then, is not whether we want information incorporated into prices—we certainly do—but how quickly and completely we want this incorporation to occur.

Consider what happens under the current prohibitionist regime. When corporate insiders acquire material nonpublic information about their companies—whether positive news like an impending breakthrough or negative developments like emerging legal troubles—they are legally barred from trading on this information. The consequence is that potentially valuable knowledge remains locked away, invisible to the market. The insider knows that the stock is undervalued or overvalued but cannot act on this knowledge. Meanwhile, ordinary investors continue making decisions based on incomplete information, and the stock price fails to reflect the reality of the company's situation.

This information blackout is not merely a theoretical concern; it has concrete and costly consequences. Studies of stock price patterns around major corporate events consistently reveal that prices continue to drift in the direction of private information for extended periods before finally incorporating that information. A pharmaceutical company awaiting FDA approval for a new drug, for instance, may see its stock price remain stagnant even as insiders know with high confidence whether approval is likely. Only when the information becomes public does the price adjust, often dramatically and suddenly. This delayed adjustment represents a failure of market efficiency—a failure that the prohibition of insider trading directly perpetuates.

Legalizing insider trading would fundamentally transform this dynamic. When insiders can legally trade on their private information, they become conduits for bringing that information into the market. Their buying signals to other investors that someone with superior knowledge sees value at current prices. Their selling signals concern about overvaluation. Either way, the information begins propagating through the market, and prices start adjusting immediately rather than waiting for formal disclosure. The result is faster, smoother, and more complete price adjustment that benefits everyone who relies on stock prices as signals for economic decision-making.

The Property Rights Argument

Beyond efficiency considerations, a powerful case for legalizing insider trading emerges from fundamental principles of property rights. Information is not a public good that belongs to everyone by default; rather, it is produced through effort, investment, and expertise. Corporate insiders who develop insights about their companies' prospects do so through their labor, their relationships, and their specialized knowledge. Why should they not have the right to profit from this valuable asset?

The current legal framework essentially confiscates the property rights of information producers. An executive who spends years building expertise in an industry, cultivating relationships that provide insight into market trends, and carefully analyzing competitive dynamics is barred from monetizing this knowledge through trading. This represents a taking of property without compensation—an infringement on the freedom to dispose of one's assets as one sees fit. The prohibition of insider trading treats information as if it belongs to the public collectively, forcing those who produce valuable insights to surrender the returns on their intellectual labor.

This property rights argument is not merely philosophical; it has practical implications for information production itself. When the returns to discovering valuable information are taxed away through criminalization, the incentive to produce such information diminishes. Why should corporate insiders invest effort in developing deep insights if they cannot profit from those insights? Why should market professionals devote resources to research and analysis if the most valuable discoveries cannot be monetized? The current regime creates systematic underinvestment in information production, leaving the market poorer for the lack of knowledge that might otherwise be created.

Legalizing insider trading would restore proper incentives for information production. Insiders would have reason to develop the deepest possible understanding of their companies and industries, knowing that valuable insights could be translated into financial returns. Market analysts and institutional investors would have stronger incentives to uncover mispriced securities, knowing that superior analysis could be exploited profitably. The result would be a richer ecosystem of information production, with more knowledge generated and more quickly incorporated into prices.

Perverse Consequences of Prohibition

The prohibition of insider trading creates not merely inefficiency in information incorporation but an array of perverse consequences that actually harm the investors it is ostensibly designed to protect. Understanding these harmful side effects strengthens the case for legalization.

First, prohibition creates incentives for information concealment rather than disclosure. Corporate insiders who cannot trade on private information have reason to hide negative developments as long as possible, delaying the incorporation of bad news into stock prices. Under the current regime, an executive who knows the company is heading for trouble is legally prohibited from selling shares, but also has no legal obligation to reveal the bad news immediately. The result is information asymmetry that is actually worse than what would exist if trading were permitted—the insider knows the truth but cannot act, while shareholders remain unaware of the looming problem. Legalizing trading would align incentives toward more prompt disclosure, since insiders would want to establish proof of their timing and demonstrate they traded on legitimate analysis rather than material nonpublic information.

Second, prohibition generates a shadow economy of illegal trading that diverts resources from productive activities. Enforcing insider trading laws requires vast expenditures by the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Department of Justice, and the financial industry itself in compliance departments, surveillance systems, and legal defense. These resources represent pure deadweight loss—they do not create value but merely prevent value transfer between private parties. Moreover, prohibition creates demand for evasion services, including encrypted communications, shell companies, and offshore accounts, all of which facilitate other forms of financial crime. Legalizing insider trading would eliminate these wasteful expenditures and remove the infrastructure that enables more serious offenses.

Third, prohibition distorts market behavior in ways that harm ordinary investors. The fear of being accused of insider trading discourages corporate insiders from trading at all, even on publicly available information. This reduces market liquidity at precisely the times when informed trading is most valuable. Institutional investors, concerned about proximity to corporate insiders, may avoid researching companies thoroughly or reduce their trading activity in affected securities. The result is a market with less information, less liquidity, and wider bid-ask spreads—all of which harm the ordinary investors that prohibition is supposedly protecting.

The Efficiency Evidence

Empirical evidence on stock market behavior supports the theoretical case for legalizing insider trading by demonstrating the efficiency benefits of informed trading. Research consistently shows that stocks with higher levels of insider buying tend to outperform in subsequent periods, suggesting that insider trading does incorporate valuable information into prices. More importantly, studies of markets with different regulatory regimes reveal that prices adjust more quickly to new information when insider trading is permitted.

The experience of jurisdictions with more permissive insider trading regimes, while limited, provides suggestive evidence of efficiency benefits. Historical analysis of markets before the development of modern insider trading enforcement suggests that price adjustment to corporate news was not noticeably worse—and was often better—than in contemporary markets with rigorous prosecution. Similarly, studies of event windows around major corporate announcements reveal that stocks continue to exhibit abnormal returns for extended periods, indicating that information is slowly incorporated over time rather than all at once. This pattern of gradual adjustment is precisely what economic theory predicts when informed traders are barred from acting.

Perhaps most compellingly, economic analysis of the costs and benefits of insider trading prohibition reveals that the costs substantially outweigh the benefits. The harm to any individual investor from insider trading is typically small—a slightly worse execution price or a brief period of trading against better-informed counterparties. The aggregate harm from delayed information incorporation, however, is substantial, affecting capital allocation throughout the economy. Regulatory enforcement consumes enormous resources without clear evidence of benefit to market quality. And the criminalization of victimless trading creates disrespect for law and undermines the legitimacy of financial regulation more broadly.

Addressing the Fairness Objection

The most powerful objection to legalizing insider trading concerns fairness. Critics argue that allowing corporate insiders to profit from private information is fundamentally unjust, creating a two-tiered system where those with access to information enjoy an advantage over ordinary investors. This objection deserves serious consideration, but ultimately fails to establish a persuasive case for prohibition.

First, perfect equality of information is neither achievable nor desirable. Some investors will always have superior resources, expertise, or relationships that give them informational advantages. A hedge fund that hires leading industry analysts will know more than a retail investor who reads only headlines. A large shareholder with a seat on the board will have insights unavailable to passive investors. The question is not whether information disparities exist—they always will—but whether the disparities that result from insider trading are particularly harmful. The evidence suggests they are not; insider trading speeds information incorporation without systematically harming other market participants.

Second, the unfairness objection conflates symmetry of information with fairness in outcomes. Even if all investors had identical information, some would make better investment decisions than others based on differing analytical abilities and risk tolerances. The fact that some investors profit from superior analysis is not generally considered unfair; we celebrate successful investors as savvy rather than criminalizing their success. Why should information derived from employment at a corporation be treated differently from information derived from proprietary research?

Third, prohibition itself creates unfairness by protecting the uninformed from consequences of their own decisions. Investors who choose to trade without researching companies accept the risk of adverse selection whenever they trade. This risk exists whether or not insider trading is legal; market professionals with superior analytical skills will always have advantages over casual investors. Legalizing insider trading would not create this asymmetry but would make it more transparent and more quickly resolved through price adjustment.

Finally, the fairness argument ignores the benefits that accrue to all market participants from faster information incorporation. When prices quickly reflect all available information, everyone makes better decisions. The retiree whose pension fund invests in index funds benefits from a market that accurately prices risk and return. The business owner who issues shares to fund expansion benefits from a market that correctly values new opportunities. The economist who studies market efficiency benefits from observing markets that actually achieve efficiency. The gains from efficient pricing are diffuse and cumulative, while the harms from insider trading are concentrated and visible. This perceptual asymmetry should not distract us from the fundamental truth that faster information incorporation helps everyone.

The Path Forward

Having established that legalizing insider trading would enhance market efficiency, respect property rights, eliminate perverse regulatory consequences, and provide diffuse benefits to all market participants, the question becomes how to implement such a reform. This would require not merely repealing existing prohibitions but establishing a new regulatory framework that maximizes the benefits of legal insider trading while addressing legitimate concerns.

A reformed legal regime should focus on disclosure rather than prohibition. Insiders should be required to report their trades promptly, allowing markets to observe and react to their signaling. This disclosure regime would be far more effective at incorporating information into prices than the current prohibition, since insiders would have strong incentives to trade and disclose when they possess valuable information. The market could then interpret these trades as signals, incorporating the information more rapidly than under current rules where insiders are barred from trading entirely.

Enforcement resources should shift from prosecuting insider trading to ensuring the integrity of disclosure systems. The SEC should focus on catching false reports, market manipulation, and other offenses that genuinely harm market participants. Resources currently devoted to proving that trades were based on material nonpublic information—a difficult and costly endeavor—could be redirected toward more productive regulatory activities.

Corporate governance should evolve to recognize insider trading as a legitimate form of compensation. Companies already compensate executives through stock options, which create obvious incentives for insider trading. Rather than pretending that executives do not trade on private information, we should establish transparent programs that allow insiders to trade within defined parameters while disclosing their activities. This would align incentives properly and reduce the current hypocrisy of penalizing behavior that option grants implicitly encourage.

Conclusion

The case for legalizing insider trading rests on solid economic foundations and survives scrutiny of the objections commonly raised against it. Far from being the nefarious practice it is commonly portrayed as, insider trading is better understood as a mechanism for accelerating information incorporation into stock prices. When informed parties can trade on their knowledge, prices adjust more quickly to reflect reality, capital allocation improves, and all market participants benefit from more efficient markets.

The prohibition of insider trading, by contrast, creates perverse incentives for information concealment, wastes resources on enforcement of questionable value, and delays the incorporation of valuable knowledge into prices. The fairness objections to legalization, while emotionally appealing, fail to establish that prohibition actually achieves fairness or that the benefits of prohibition outweigh its costs.

Reforming insider trading law will require challenging deeply held beliefs about market fairness and overcoming the political appeal of appearing tough on financial crime. Yet the economic case for reform is compelling. Markets work better when information flows freely, and legalizing insider trading is the most direct path to faster, more complete information incorporation. It is time to recognize that the Emperor has no clothes—that our conventional wisdom about insider trading is wrong, and that legalization would make our markets more efficient, more productive, and more just.

The Case for Free Information: A Defense of Insider Trading

Ladies and gentlemen, distinguished economists, fellow believers in the power of free markets:

We gather today to challenge one of the most sacred cows of financial regulation—to question a prohibition that has been accepted without serious scrutiny for nearly a century, and to ask a radical question: What if the ban on insider trading is not a protection of investors, but an impediment to prosperity? I stand before you to make the case for the complete legalization of insider trading—not because I wish to reward the privileged, but because I believe in the radical principle that information wants to be free, that markets work best when information flows fastest, and that the moralizing impulse behind our current prohibitions has done more harm than the practice it seeks to prevent.

The Myth of the Level Playing Field

Let us begin with the fundamental lie at the heart of insider trading prohibition: the fiction of the level playing field. We are told that insider trading is unfair because some traders have information that others do not. But I ask you: has there ever been a market, in the entire history of human commerce, where all participants possessed equal information? Of course not. Such a market is a fantasy—a theoretical abstraction that exists only in the minds of regulators who wish to impose their vision of fairness upon the messy reality of economic life.

The investor who rises at five in the morning to study quarterly reports has information that the investor who sleeps until noon does not. The analyst who spends decades understanding the nuances of a particular industry has information that the casual observer lacks. The trader with superior mathematical models, faster computer connections, or deeper relationships with corporate management—all of these participants possess advantages that others do not. We do not ban early rising, or expertise, or technological advantage. Why, then, do we ban the possession of material non-public information?

The honest answer is that we cannot ban information advantages without destroying markets entirely. Every piece of analysis, every insight, every prediction is, in some sense, information that someone else does not have. The prohibition on insider trading is not creating fairness—it is arbitrarily criminalizing a particular category of information advantage, one that happens to involve corporate insiders, while leaving all other advantages perfectly legal.

Information as the Lifeblood of Markets

Consider what markets actually do. At their core, markets are information-processing machines. The price of a stock is not merely a number—it is a condensation of countless pieces of knowledge about a company's prospects, its management, its competitors, its industry, and the broader economy. When information changes, prices should change. The faster information flows into prices, the more accurately prices reflect reality, and the better capital is allocated in our economy.

This is the fundamental insight that insider trading prohibition obscures. When corporate insiders trade on material non-public information, they are not engaging in fraud—they are performing a vital economic function. They are taking information that exists in the hands of a few and incorporating it into market prices, where it benefits everyone who owns stock, everyone who manages pension funds, everyone who participates in the economy.

Imagine a pharmaceutical company has just discovered that its flagship drug has failed clinical trials. The executives know this information before the public does. Under current law, if they sell their stock before the news becomes public, they go to prison. But what is the actual harm? They have recognized that the value of their company has declined, and they have sold their shares at a price that still reflects the old, higher value. They have, in effect, transferred wealth to the unsuspecting buyers of their stock. Is this unfair to the buyers? Perhaps. But consider what has happened to the market: these executives have sold so much stock that the price has begun to fall, even before the official announcement. Other investors notice the unusual selling and begin to ask questions. The information has begun to flow into prices faster than it would have otherwise.

This is not a bug of insider trading—it is a feature. Insiders have the most accurate information about their companies. When they trade on that information, they are performing the valuable service of updating market prices more quickly than would otherwise occur. Every investor benefits from more accurate prices, even if they never trade a single share.

The Inefficiency of Prohibition

Now let us examine the practical effects of our current prohibition. We have created a vast enforcement apparatus—the Securities and Exchange Commission, elaborate surveillance systems, armies of compliance officers—all devoted to policing a activity that is difficult to define, even more difficult to detect, and inconsistently punished. The definitions of "material" and "non-public" information are famously vague, creating a chilling effect that extends far beyond actual wrongdoers. Executives who might otherwise buy or sell their company's stock at the optimal time—performing that valuable price-discovery function—instead hesitate, uncertain whether their trades will later be deemed illegal.

Consider the paradox at the heart of our current system. We want corporate insiders to disclose material information promptly and completely. But when they do disclose it, the market often overreacts or underreacts, because the information has been released in a controlled, stylized format rather than through the natural process of trading. The elegant mechanism of continuous price discovery, which has evolved over centuries of market history, is replaced by a theatrical performance of press releases and conference calls.

Moreover, the prohibition on insider trading has not eliminated insider trading—it has merely driven it underground. Those with the most to gain from trading on inside information—the sophisticated, the connected, the well-advised—continue to do so, while the SEC's enforcement actions serve primarily to demonstrate the law's reach rather than its effectiveness. Meanwhile, the rest of us, the ordinary investors who are supposedly protected by these laws, are left with a system that is more opaque, more legalistic, and no more fair than the alternatives.

The Paternalistic Fallacy

Behind the prohibition on insider trading lies a deeply paternalistic assumption: that ordinary investors need to be protected from their own decisions, that the government must ensure that no one gains an advantage that others cannot obtain, that markets must be artificially equalized to protect participants from their own lack of information or sophistication.

This assumption is not merely condescending—it is economically destructive. We do not ban expert cardiologists from performing heart surgery simply because most people cannot perform surgery themselves. We do not require that all legal arguments be presented by people without legal training, to ensure a "level playing field" in the courtroom. We recognize that expertise and information advantages are not just inevitable but valuable—they are the engine of progress and specialization.

The same should be true in markets. The person who knows more, who works harder, who has better access to information—that person should be rewarded for that advantage. This is not a bug in market capitalism; it is the very essence of market capitalism. We want capital to flow to those who can put it to most productive use, and that requires that those with better information be able to act on that information.

A Vision of Information Freedom

Imagine, for a moment, a different world. In this world, there are no laws against insider trading. Corporate executives trade their company's stock freely, whenever they believe the price is right. Academic researchers who discover insights about companies are free to trade on those insights. Journalists who uncover stories can act on their information. The market is a free-for-all of information acquisition and trading, governed only by the general laws against fraud and deception—lying about what you know is still illegal, but merely knowing something that others do not know is not.

What would this market look like? It would be faster, more efficient, more responsive to real information. Prices would adjust more quickly to changing circumstances, reducing the misallocation of capital that occurs when prices fail to reflect available knowledge. The divide between "insiders" and "outsiders" would blur, because everyone would be free to acquire and act on information through whatever means were available to them. The artificial boundary between legal and illegal information—between what you can know and what you can trade on—would disappear.

Would there be abuses? Of course. Fraud would still be illegal, and fraudsters would still be punished. Some people would still try to deceive others about what they know. But these abuses exist today despite our elaborate prohibition on insider trading, and they would exist in any system. The question is whether we want to supplement our existing anti-fraud laws with an additional prohibition that criminalizes a broad category of information use while failing to prevent the abuses it is supposed to address.

Conclusion: Freedom to Trade, Freedom to Know

Ladies and gentlemen:

I ask you to reconsider what you have been taught about insider trading. I ask you to look past the moral rhetoric—past the language of "fairness" and "level playing fields" that sounds appealing but obscures more than it reveals. I ask you to consider the economic function of trading on information, the value of rapid price discovery, and the ways in which our current prohibition impedes the very efficiency it claims to promote.

The case for legalizing insider trading is ultimately a case for human freedom—the freedom to acquire information, to act on knowledge, to participate fully in the economic life of our society without asking permission from regulators who cannot possibly know what information is valuable and when. It is a case for trusting markets to process information more efficiently than any regulatory apparatus ever could.

We have tried prohibition for nearly a century, and what do we have to show for it? A compliance industry worth billions, enforcement actions that are arbitrary and inconsistent, and markets that are no fairer or more efficient than they would be under a regime of information freedom. It is time to try something different. It is time to recognize that information is not a privilege to be hoarded but a resource to be shared, that markets work best when information flows fastest, and that freedom—however messy and however uncomfortable to those who prefer the illusion of control—is the ultimate foundation of prosperity.

Let us end the war on insider trading. Let us trust the market. Let us set information free.

The Case for Legalizing Insider Trading: Enhancing Market Efficiency Through Information Flow

Introduction

The prohibition of insider trading has long been a cornerstone of securities regulation in most developed economies. However, this essay argues that fully legalizing insider trading would be beneficial to financial markets and society at large. At the core of this argument is the contention that allowing insider trading enhances market efficiency by speeding up the incorporation of private information into stock prices. Rather than being a threat to market integrity, insider trading can serve as a mechanism that improves price discovery, allocates capital more efficiently, and reduces market distortions. This essay will examine the economic, informational, and practical arguments supporting the full legalization of insider trading.

The Information Efficiency Argument

The most compelling case for legalizing insider trading lies in its ability to improve market efficiency through faster information dissemination. Financial markets function optimally when securities prices accurately reflect all available information. Currently, there exists an artificial delay between when material information becomes known internally and when it becomes public. This delay creates inefficient pricing periods that can last days or weeks.

When insiders trade on non-public information, their actions begin moving prices toward levels that reflect the true value of the securities even before public announcements. This price adjustment happens gradually as insider transactions signal information to other market participants. As economist Henry Manne argued in his seminal work "Insider Trading and the Stock Market," insider trading serves as a rapid information transmission mechanism that benefits market participants by reducing the period during which securities are mispriced.

Consider a company that has discovered a significant new product or encountered a major liability. Under current regulations, this information remains walled off from the market until formal disclosure, creating an artificial pricing environment. Allowing insiders to trade would create subtle but meaningful price signals that would reduce these inefficiencies and allow for more accurate capital allocation throughout the economy.

Reducing Market Volatility

A counterintuitive benefit of legalizing insider trading would be reduced market volatility. Currently, material information is released through formalized announcements, leading to dramatic price adjustments as the market rapidly processes new information. These sudden movements create price shocks that can trigger panic selling, algorithm-based trading cascades, and market disruption.

If insider trading were permitted, material information would gradually filter into prices ahead of formal announcements. By the time public disclosure occurs, prices would already partially reflect the new information, reducing the magnitude of sudden price swings. This smoother price discovery process would benefit all market participants by creating more orderly markets with fewer dramatic gaps and corrections.

The False Promise of Equal Information

Regulations prohibiting insider trading are often justified on fairness grounds, suggesting that all participants deserve equal access to information. However, this notion is fundamentally at odds with how markets actually function. Perfect information equality is neither achievable nor necessarily desirable in complex financial markets.

Information asymmetry already exists widely in legal forms. Institutional investors employ teams of analysts, maintain networks of industry experts, and utilize sophisticated data analytics that give them substantial advantages over retail investors. High-frequency traders gain advantages through speed and technological sophistication. The current system permits vast information disparities while arbitrarily prohibiting one specific type.

Legalizing insider trading would acknowledge the reality that information asymmetry is an inherent part of markets. Instead of creating an illusion of equality, it would focus on the more important goal of ensuring that information—regardless of its source—is incorporated into prices as efficiently as possible, improving market function for all participants.

Practical Enforcement Challenges

The current prohibition regime faces significant practical challenges. Enforcement is inconsistent, expensive, and often appears arbitrary. The line between illegal insider information and legal market research has become increasingly blurred. Analysts routinely speak with company executives, suppliers, and customers to gain information edges that approach but presumably don't cross regulatory boundaries.

This gray area creates legal uncertainty while consuming substantial regulatory resources. The SEC must devote significant capacity to insider trading cases that could be better directed toward addressing more harmful financial crimes such as Ponzi schemes, accounting fraud, and market manipulation that directly harm investors.

Legalizing insider trading would eliminate this regulatory quagmire, allowing for more efficient allocation of enforcement resources toward unambiguous forms of market misconduct that involve actual deception rather than information advantages.

Market-Based Solutions to Potential Concerns

Critics of legalizing insider trading raise legitimate concerns about potential negative effects on corporate governance and shareholder interests. However, market-based solutions would likely emerge to address these issues more efficiently than the current regulatory approach.

Companies concerned about information leakage could implement internal trading policies, contractual restrictions on executives, or compensation structures that discourage short-term trading by insiders. Shareholders could demand such protections through corporate governance mechanisms, and companies offering stronger protections might command premium valuations.

This market-based approach would allow for experimentation with different policies tailored to specific company circumstances rather than imposing a one-size-fits-all regulatory prohibition. Some companies might determine that allowing freer information flow through insider trading better serves their capital market goals, while others might implement stricter internal controls.

Conclusion

Fully legalizing insider trading represents a market-oriented approach that acknowledges the central importance of information in efficient price discovery. The current prohibition regime creates artificial delays in information incorporation, increases market volatility, and consumes regulatory resources that could be better deployed elsewhere.

By allowing insider trading, markets would benefit from enhanced efficiency as private information more rapidly influences stock prices. The result would be more accurate asset pricing, better capital allocation, and reduced market distortions. Rather than clinging to the illusion of information equality, regulators should embrace a system that prioritizes the rapid and efficient incorporation of all information into market prices, regardless of its source.

While this position challenges longstanding regulatory orthodoxy, it is grounded in sound economic principles regarding how information functions in markets. The ultimate goal of financial regulation should be to create the most efficient, well-functioning markets possible—and legalizing insider trading would be a significant step toward achieving that objective.

The Case for Fully Legalizing Insider Trading: Markets Work Best When Information Flows Free

Every participant in a financial market is trying to do precisely one thing: trade on information that other people do not yet have. The analyst who reads a thousand pages of filings, the fund manager who visits factories and counts cars in parking lots, the quant who mines satellite images of shipping lanes—all of them are hunting for an informational edge, and we celebrate them for it. Yet when the person holding the superior information happens to be a corporate insider, we call the identical conduct a felony. This is an incoherent distinction, and it imposes real costs on markets, on investors, and on the economy. Insider trading should be fully legalized—not regulated around the edges, not reformed, but legalized—because allowing insider trading enhances market efficiency by speeding up the incorporation of private information into stock prices, because it is a powerful and efficient form of compensation for value creators, because the prohibition rests on a victimless conception of harm, and because the current legal regime is an unenforceable doctrinal mess that criminalizes an activity markets cannot function without.

Prices Are Signals, and Insiders Make Them Accurate

The foundational insight belongs to Henry Manne, whose 1966 book Insider Trading and the Stock Market first dared to defend the indefensible. A stock price is not merely a number; it is a signal that directs capital throughout the entire economy. When prices are accurate, capital flows to its most productive uses. When prices are wrong, the economy misallocates trillions of dollars. The whole purpose of a market is to aggregate information into prices, and anything that accelerates that aggregation is a public good.

Under the current regime, material information reaches prices in violent lurches. A pharmaceutical company completes a successful drug trial, sits on the results for weeks, and then announces them on a Tuesday morning—at which point the stock gaps up forty percent in seconds. Everyone who sold shares in the preceding weeks sold at a price the market knew was wrong. Everyone who bought during the announcement chaos bought into a stampede. Now consider the alternative. If insiders could trade freely, they would begin buying as soon as the trial results were known. Their buying would push the price upward, day by day, toward its true level. By the time the public announcement arrived, the price would already reflect the news. The announcement-day crash-or-spike would largely disappear.

Notice who benefits: every single investor who traded during that window. The retirees selling shares to fund their expenses would have sold at prices closer to true value. The index funds buying would have bought into a market whose prices meant something. Skeptics can observe this dynamic in the wild today—prices notoriously "run up" before merger announcements, precisely because information leaks through trading. That run-up is not a scandal; it is the market working, imperfectly and illegally, the way it should work openly. Legalizing insider trading would simply let prices do their job faster, smoothing today's destabilizing price discontinuities into gradual, information-rich adjustments.

The Ideal Compensation for People Who Create Value

Manne's second argument deserves equal weight: insider trading is a nearly perfect compensation mechanism for entrepreneurs and executives. Consider what we want from executive pay. We want to reward people specifically for increasing the value of the firm, and we want the reward to arrive in proportion to the value created. Stock options attempt this crudely, but they reward market-wide tides as much as individual contribution, and they can be gamed by timing grants and announcements. Insider trading profits, by contrast, are available to an executive only when she has genuinely created value that the market has not yet recognized. The engineer-executive whose breakthrough will double the company's worth can capture a slice of the very value she built. The cash-poor startup can pay visionary talent in information rather than salary it cannot afford.

Critics object that insiders could also profit from bad news by selling or shorting. But this is a feature, not a bug. Today, an executive who discovers a serious problem has every incentive to delay disclosure while the stock stays inflated. In a legalized regime, the executive profits by moving quickly—by trading on the truth before anyone else, which pushes the price toward reality and effectively forces disclosure through the price itself. The incentive structure flips from concealment to rapid revelation.

A Crime Without a Victim

Ask who is injured when an insider buys stock, and the question collapses under scrutiny. In an anonymous electronic market, the seller placed her sell order independently. She wanted to sell at $50; the insider's buy order filled her at $50—or, because informed buying increases demand, perhaps at $50.10. Her decision was not caused by the insider; if anything, the insider improved her execution price. The "injury" is purely counterfactual: she would have held the stock had she known what the insider knew. But no legal system in any other domain recognizes a right to other people's knowledge. A buyer who purchases land knowing a highway is coming commits no fraud. A dealer who recognizes an undervalued antique at a yard sale owes the seller nothing. Only in securities markets have we invented the bizarre principle that trading while better informed is theft—and even there, we apply it selectively, since the analyst with the superior model and the hedge fund with the satellite data trade legally every day.

The Fairness Objection Misses the Point of Markets

The emotional core of the prohibition is fairness: insider trading feels like cheating. But markets have never offered equal information, and they are not supposed to. The retail investor with a phone app competes against institutions with Bloomberg terminals, proprietary data feeds, and floors of PhDs. If informational equality were the goal, we would have to ban research itself. The actual purpose of capital markets is efficient capital allocation, and that purpose is served, not undermined, by participants who push prices toward truth. As for the claim that legalization would destroy investor confidence and liquidity: confidence ultimately rests on the belief that prices are meaningful. A market where prices jump forty percent on press releases because information was suppressed for weeks is not obviously more trustworthy than one where prices drift smoothly toward reality. Investors who fear being on the wrong side of informed trades can hold diversified index funds—and their returns will still benefit from a market whose prices are continuously trued by the best-informed traders in it.

An Unenforceable Law Is Worse Than No Law

Even setting principle aside, the current regime fails on its own terms. The United States has no statute defining insider trading. The prohibition was constructed by courts out of anti-fraud doctrine, leaving the actual crime defined by a shifting body of case law: Who owes a duty to whom? What counts as a "personal benefit" to a tipper? The Supreme Court's own decisions—from Chiarella to Dirks to Salman—read like a decades-long confession that no one can state the rule in advance. The Dirks case reaches the absurdity's apex: the government prosecuted an analyst whose "tip" exposed one of the largest corporate frauds in American history. Meanwhile, the "mosaic theory" permits analysts to assemble material conclusions from bits of non-public information—so non-public knowledge is legal or illegal depending not on its content but on its source, a distinction with no economic logic. The result is selective enforcement, chilling effects on legitimate research, enormous compliance costs, and a criminal law that citizens cannot know they are obeying. A prohibition this incoherent is not a rule of law; it is a lottery with prison terms.

The Sensible Endgame: Legalize, Disclose, and Let Firms Choose

The strongest version of the proposal answers the remaining objections by design. Legalize insider trading as a default rule. Require insiders to disclose their trades in real time rather than on the current lagged schedule, so the market sees informed money moving instantly. And—crucially—permit corporations to restrict insider trading by contract if they believe it harms them. This final point is devastating to the prohibitionist case: if insider trading genuinely injured shareholders, companies would ban it in their charters and employment agreements, and enforcement would be an ordinary matter of contract law. The supposed victims would protect themselves at trivial cost. That we instead require an army of federal prosecutors suggests the harm was always mythical. Conclusion

Markets are information-processing machines. Their prices guide the allocation of capital across the entire economy, and those prices are only as good as the information they absorb. For over half a century, we have criminalized the participation of the best-informed traders, forcing prices to lurch between ignorance and revelation while pretending that an arbitrary line between "legitimate research" and "illicit knowledge" marks the boundary of morality. It does not. Legalizing insider trading would accelerate the incorporation of private information into prices, reward the people who actually create corporate value, end a victimless prosecution regime that cannot even define its own crime, and replace paternalistic prohibition with disclosure and private contracting. The free flow of information is not a threat to markets. It is what markets are for. It is time the law stopped punishing them for working.

The central argument draws on Hayek's insight that prices are information-aggregation mechanisms—markets coordinate dispersed knowledge that no central authority could assemble. From this view:

  • Smoother adjustment: If insiders gradually sell after learning of, say, a failed drug trial, the price declines incrementally rather than collapsing in a single shock when the news breaks. Proponents argue this reduces disruptive volatility.

A related point (echoing Grossman-Stiglitz logic): information is only produced and incorporated into prices because trading on it is profitable. Restricting who may profit from information reduces the incentive to generate and reveal it, degrading the informational content of prices for everyone.

2. Efficient Compensation and Entrepreneurial Incentives

Manne argued that insider trading profits function as a compensation mechanism for entrepreneurs and managers who create value. 3. The "No Identifiable Victim" Argument

Proponents argue the fairness intuition underlying prohibition doesn't map cleanly onto markets where counterparties are strangers whose decisions are independent of the insider's.

4. Private Contracting Beats One-Size-Fits-All Regulation

Economists like Dennis Carlton and Daniel Fischel made a Coasean argument: if insider trading genuinely harms a firm's shareholders, firms have every incentive to prohibit it in corporate charters and employment contracts.
